questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a platelet count of 980 ×10⁹/L on a routine blood test, and the same on repeat 3 months later. He feels well. He has no infection, bleeding or recent surgery. His spleen is just palpable. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A persistently raised platelet count with no reactive cause, found incidentally, points to essential thrombocythaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: no infection, bleeding or recent surgery
steps.x: Persistent, unexplained, isolated thrombocytosis.

elim: Would show a raised white cell count with left shift.
Usually causes cytopenias, especially anaemia, not isolated thrombocytosis.
His haemoglobin is normal.
No infection, inflammation, bleeding or iron deficiency; CRP and ferritin are normal.

steps.x: **B. Essential thrombocythaemia.** Raised platelets with no reactive cause = ET.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness, weight loss and sweats. She is pale and her spleen is palpable to the right iliac fossa. Her liver is also enlarged. Investigations: haemoglobin 82 g/L (115–165), white cell count 2.9 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) and platelets 88 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Her blood film shows nucleated red cells, myelocytes and teardrop cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pancytopenia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, constitutional symptoms and a leukoerythroblastic film with teardrop cells are primary myelofibrosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: spleen is palpable to the right iliac fossa
nucleated red cells, myelocytes and teardrop cells
steps.x: Massive spleen plus marrow failure plus leukoerythroblastic film with dacrocytes.

elim: The film would show blasts, and a massive spleen is not typical.
Causes a very high white cell count, not pancytopenia.
Causes cytopenias but not massive hepatosplenomegaly with teardrop cells.
Raises haemoglobin rather than causing anaemia.

steps.x: **E. Primary myelofibrosis.** Massive spleen + pancytopenia + teardrop cells = PMF.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 2 months of headaches, lightheadedness and episodes of atypical chest pain. She fainted once last week. Her ECG and troponin are normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (115–165), white cell count 7.9 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) and platelets 1,150 ×10⁹/L (150–400). A JAK2 V617F mutation is detected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: ET causes headache, lightheadedness, syncope and atypical chest pain from dysfunctional platelets in the microcirculation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: headaches, lightheadedness and episodes of atypical chest pain
steps.x: Isolated very high platelets with JAK2 and microvascular symptoms.

elim: Causes a low platelet count.
Haemoglobin is normal.
Would show anaemia, a massive spleen and teardrop cells.
Does not carry a JAK2 mutation, and no infection or inflammation is described.

steps.x: **A. Essential thrombocythaemia.** ET symptoms: headache, lightheadedness, syncope, atypical chest pain, erythromelalgia.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is found to have a platelet count of 1,240 ×10⁹/L. His haemoglobin and white cell count are normal, ferritin and CRP are normal, and a JAK2 V617F mutation is detected. A blood film is examined.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
questions.e: In ET the high platelet count comes with giant platelets and platelet clumps on the film.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
JAK2-positive isolated thrombocytosis is ET.

elim: Seen in acute myeloid leukaemia.
Fragmented red cells of microangiopathic haemolysis.
Seen in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Seen in liver disease, thalassaemia and after splenectomy.

steps.x: **A. Giant platelets and platelet clumps.** ET film: giant platelets and clumps.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with essential thrombocythaemia stopped her medication 3 months ago because of indigestion. She suddenly develops weakness of her right arm and leg and slurred speech. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and regular and BP 150/88 mmHg. Her platelet count is 1,380 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ET carries a major risk of arterial thrombosis, including ischaemic stroke, especially when untreated.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Untreated ET with very high platelets and sudden focal deficit.

elim: Affects only the face, without limb weakness or dysarthria.
No diabetes treatment; a very high platelet count points to thrombosis.
Sudden fixed hemiparesis at 68 is a stroke until proven otherwise.
Usually gradual with confusion after a fall.

steps.x: **C. Ischaemic stroke.** ET complications: arterial and venous thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT, PE).

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with polycythaemia vera has missed his venesection appointments for 6 months. He now has headache, blurred vision, tinnitus and mild confusion. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 164/92 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows dilated, tortuous retinal veins. His haematocrit is 0.62 (0.40–0.52).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Very high red cell mass raises blood viscosity, giving headache, visual disturbance, tinnitus and confusion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Untreated PV with a very high haematocrit and neurological symptoms.

elim: His BP is only modestly raised and the haematocrit explains the picture.
Does not cause dilated retinal veins.
No fever or neck stiffness.
Causes gait, cognitive and urinary problems over months.

steps.x: **B. Hyperviscosity.** MPN complications include hyperviscosity symptoms.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has itching after hot showers and a red face. Her spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Investigations: haemoglobin 192 g/L (115–165), white cell count 13.2 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 520 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and low serum erythropoietin. Genetic testing is sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on genetic testing?
questions.e: Myeloproliferative disorders, especially polycythaemia vera, are associated with the JAK2 V617F mutation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Aquagenic itch, high Hb, raised other cell lines and low EPO: polycythaemia vera.

elim: The Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
Mantle cell lymphoma and some myeloma.
A poor-prognosis lesion in CLL and other cancers, not the driver of an MPN.

steps.x: **A. JAK2 V617F mutation.** PV, ET and PMF: JAK2 V617F.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has 4 months of fatigue, night sweats and feeling full after only a few mouthfuls of food. He has a dragging feeling in his left upper abdomen. His blood count shows a raised white cell count and platelets, and a JAK2 mutation is found.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: MPNs commonly cause splenomegaly, giving early satiety and abdominal fullness, with constitutional symptoms.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: feeling full after only a few mouthfuls
dragging feeling in his left upper abdomen
steps.x: Early satiety and left upper quadrant fullness in a JAK2-positive MPN.

elim: Not typical; fullness and dragging left-sided discomfort point to the spleen.
Suggests lymphoma or CLL, not an MPN.
Seen in monocytic acute leukaemia.
Suggests liver metastases.

steps.x: **E. Splenomegaly.** MPN: splenomegaly, early satiety, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has had essential thrombocythaemia for 12 years. Over 6 months she has become tired and her spleen has grown to 10 cm below the costal margin. Her platelet count has fallen from 900 to 140 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and her haemoglobin is 88 g/L (115–165). The film shows teardrop cells. There are no blasts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: ET (and PV) can progress over time to myelofibrosis, with falling counts, splenomegaly and teardrop cells.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Long-standing MPN, now marrow failure with a growing spleen and dacrocytes but no blasts.

elim: Causes cytopenias but not a growing spleen with teardrop cells.
Would not cause anaemia, a large spleen or teardrop cells.
Causes microcytosis, not splenomegaly and teardrop cells.
There are no blasts on the film.

steps.x: **D. Progression to myelofibrosis.** MPN progression: myelofibrosis (teardrop cells) or AML (blasts).

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 3 months of nosebleeds and easy bruising. She takes no medication. Her spleen is not palpable. Investigations: haemoglobin 134 g/L (115–165), white cell count 7.4 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 1,680 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Clotting is normal and a JAK2 V617F mutation is detected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ET causes bleeding as well as thrombosis because the many platelets are dysfunctional, particularly at very high counts.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Bleeding despite a very high platelet count, with JAK2.

elim: White cell count is normal and JAK2 is present.
Would prolong the APTT; clotting is normal.
Causes bleeding from a low, not high, platelet count.
Does not carry a JAK2 mutation.

steps.x: **B. Essential thrombocythaemia.** ET: bleeding and thrombosis with a raised platelet count.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with primary myelofibrosis and massive splenomegaly has sudden severe left upper quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder tip. It is worse on breathing in. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. There is a left upper quadrant friction rub and tenderness over the spleen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A massive spleen in myelofibrosis outgrows its blood supply and can infarct, causing acute left upper quadrant pain and a friction rub.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: radiating to the left shoulder tip
steps.x: Massive spleen with sudden pleuritic LUQ pain and a rub.

elim: Epigastric pain radiating to the back.
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals.
Would cause cough and chest signs rather than a splenic rub.
Causes peritonism and a rigid abdomen, not a splenic friction rub.

steps.x: **E. Splenic infarction.** Massive splenomegaly in PMF: risk of splenic infarction and other splenic complications.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 3 months of headaches and itching after a bath. His face looks red. He has never smoked and has no lung or heart disease. His pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 148/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His GP suspects a myeloproliferative disorder.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A full blood count comes first, to show which cell line is high.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Suspected MPN; nothing has been measured yet.

elim: Specialist test after the blood count and JAK2 result.
Not a first test; it does not show which cell line is raised.
Follows once the blood count shows a raised cell line.
Helps separate PV from secondary causes once a high Hb is found.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** First-line in suspected MPN: FBC to see which line is raised.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has massive splenomegaly, anaemia and teardrop cells on his blood film. A bone marrow aspirate yields no cells ('dry tap'), so a trephine biopsy is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the trephine biopsy?
o: Marrow fibrosis within a collagenous matrix
questions.e: In primary myelofibrosis the trephine shows marrow fibrosis, with marrow that may be hyperplastic or hypoplastic, embedded in a collagenous matrix.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Dry tap plus dacrocytes and a big spleen is myelofibrosis.

elim: Diagnostic of acute leukaemia.
Suggests myeloma.
Seen in sideroblastic anaemia and some myelodysplasia.
Suggests tuberculosis.

steps.x: **A. Marrow fibrosis within a collagenous matrix.** PMF is diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a haemoglobin of 196 g/L (130–180) and haematocrit of 0.58 (0.40–0.52). His white cell count and platelets are normal. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, has no lung disease and his oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air. JAK2 testing is pending.
questions.q: Which other blood test best helps distinguish polycythaemia vera from a secondary cause?
questions.e: Low EPO suggests PV (EPO-independent production); raised EPO suggests a secondary cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Raised Hb with a possible secondary cause (smoking).

elim: Shows iron stores, not the cause of erythrocytosis.
Shows cell turnover but does not separate primary from secondary.
May be raised in either.
Not useful in this question.

steps.x: **C. Serum erythropoietin.** EPO level: low in PV, high in secondary polycythaemia.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a platelet count of 870 ×10⁹/L on three blood tests over 4 months. Iron studies and CRP are normal. She is referred to haematology to confirm the diagnosis of a myeloproliferative disorder.
questions.q: Which combination of tests is the gold standard for diagnosis?
o: FBC, mutation testing and bone marrow assessment
questions.e: MPNs are confirmed by FBC, mutation testing (JAK2) and a haematology workup with marrow assessment.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Reactive causes are excluded; she needs a confirmatory workup.

elim: Inflammatory markers only exclude reactive causes.
A staging scan for solid cancer, not MPN diagnosis.
Assess thrombosis or coagulopathy, not the MPN itself.
Not enough to confirm a clonal disorder.

steps.x: **D. FBC, mutation testing and bone marrow assessment.** MPN diagnosis: FBC + JAK2 (mutation) testing + marrow assessment.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with primary myelofibrosis has fatigue, night sweats and a massive spleen. He also has painful swelling of his right big toe. Investigations are shown, including a raised lactate dehydrogenase.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional biochemical finding?
o: Raised serum bilirubin with raised ALP
questions.e: High cell turnover in MPNs raises LDH and urate, which can cause gout.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.

clues: painful swelling of his right big toe
steps.x: High turnover marrow disease plus acute gout.

elim: Not a feature of myelofibrosis.
Not linked to marrow turnover.
Suggests pancreatitis.
A cholestatic liver picture, not the toe or marrow disease.

steps.x: **E. Raised serum urate.** MPN workup includes LDH and urate (both raised by high cell turnover).

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has pancytopenia and a spleen palpable 12 cm below the costal margin. She has lost 6 kg. A blood film is reviewed by the haematologist before a marrow biopsy is planned.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
o: Nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells
questions.e: In myelofibrosis the film shows a leukoerythroblastic picture (nucleated red cells and immature white cells) with teardrop cells.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Pancytopenia with a massive spleen suggests myelofibrosis.

elim: Oxidative haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
B12 or folate deficiency.
Iron deficiency anaemia.
Hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis.

steps.x: **C. Nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells.** PMF film: leukoerythroblastic picture + dacrocytes.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has essential thrombocythaemia confirmed by JAK2 testing. Her platelet count is 1,100 ×10⁹/L (150–400). She has had no thrombosis or bleeding. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Her renal and liver function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: In ET, low-dose aspirin is first line; high-risk patients (such as over 60, previous thrombosis, very high count) also need cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Older age, very high count and vascular risk factors make her high risk.

elim: Not enough for a high-risk patient (over 60 with a very high count).
She is high risk for thrombosis.
Treats polycythaemia vera, not a raised platelet count.
Not used for primary prevention in ET.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin and hydroxycarbamide.** ET: aspirin for all; add hydroxycarbamide if high risk.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with essential thrombocythaemia has episodes of burning pain and redness in her fingers and toes, relieved by cooling them. She has had no thrombosis or bleeding. Her platelet count is 780 ×10⁹/L (150–400). She takes no medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for her symptoms?
questions.e: Erythromelalgia in ET is caused by dysfunctional platelets and responds to low-dose aspirin, which is also first-line therapy.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: burning pain and redness in her fingers and toes
steps.x: Erythromelalgia in low-risk ET.

elim: A neuropathic pain drug; it does not treat platelet-driven symptoms.
Does not treat erythromelalgia from platelet activation.
May worsen peripheral blood flow.
Treats polycythaemia vera.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin 75 mg daily.** ET first line: low-dose aspirin, which also relieves erythromelalgia.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with essential thrombocythaemia had a DVT a year ago. His platelet count is 1,250 ×10⁹/L despite aspirin. Hydroxycarbamide is started. He asks what it is meant to do.
questions.q: Which is the intended effect of hydroxycarbamide?
o: Destroy circulating platelets in the spleen
questions.e: Hydroxycarbamide is a cytoreductive drug that suppresses platelet production in high-risk ET.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: had a DVT a year ago
steps.x: High risk (previous thrombosis, high count): cytoreduction.

elim: The action of aspirin, which he already takes.
Not its action.
That is thrombolysis.
The action of DOACs.

steps.x: **E. Suppress platelet production.** Hydroxycarbamide = cytoreduction, reducing platelet production.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has intermediate-risk primary myelofibrosis. His massive spleen causes early satiety and discomfort, and he has night sweats and weight loss. His haemoglobin is 112 g/L. He is frail and not fit for a stem cell transplant.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate targeted therapy?
questions.e: Targeted therapy for symptomatic PMF is a JAK inhibitor such as ruxolitinib, which reduces spleen size and constitutional symptoms.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: not fit for a stem cell transplant
steps.x: Symptomatic splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms, transplant not possible.

elim: Does not shrink the spleen or treat symptoms.
A BCR-ABL1 inhibitor for chronic myeloid leukaemia.
An anti-CD20 antibody for B-cell disease.
Would worsen his anaemia; used in PV.

steps.x: **D. Ruxolitinib.** PMF: supportive care, cytoreduction, JAK inhibitor (ruxolitinib), transplant if fit.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man sees his GP with fatigue and drenching night sweats. His spleen is palpable 8 cm below the costal margin. His full blood count shows haemoglobin 96 g/L (130–180) and platelets 110 ×10⁹/L (150–400). He has no fever, cough or lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral iron and recheck in 3 months
Reassure and repeat the blood count in 6 months
questions.e: Splenomegaly with cytopenias and constitutional symptoms suggests a myeloproliferative disorder such as myelofibrosis, which needs specialist haematology workup and care.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Constitutional symptoms, big spleen and cytopenias.

elim: Delays diagnosis of a likely marrow disorder.
Does not address the diagnosis and is risky with low platelets.
Splenomegaly with cytopenias needs prompt review.
No diagnosis to treat.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to haematology.** Suspected MPN: refer to haematology for workup and specialist care.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has polycythaemia vera with a JAK2 V617F mutation. A student asks what kind of protein JAK2 is and why the mutation lets cells divide without normal growth signals.
questions.q: Which best describes JAK2?
o: A cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase in cytokine signalling
questions.e: JAK2 is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase linked to cytokine receptors; V617F makes it constitutively active, so JAK-STAT signalling drives cytokine-independent proliferation.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
The mutation switches on a signalling enzyme permanently.

elim: That describes p53 or Rb, not JAK2.
Not the function of JAK2.
JAK2 is not a channel.
JAK2 signals via STAT transcription factors, but is itself a kinase.

steps.x: **B. A cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase in cytokine signalling.** JAK2 = tyrosine kinase; V617F gives constitutive JAK-STAT activation.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a raised haemoglobin, raised white cell count and raised platelets. A JAK2 V617F mutation is found in her granulocytes, red cell precursors and megakaryocytes. She asks why all three blood cell types are affected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Clonal disorder of a haematopoietic stem cell
questions.e: MPNs are clonal neoplastic disorders of a haematopoietic stem cell, so the mutation is in all its descendant cell lines.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: granulocytes, red cell precursors and megakaryocytes
steps.x: The same mutation appears in several lineages: they share an ancestor.

elim: No autoimmune process causes this pattern.
Would raise red cells only.
Would raise platelets only.
Would not cause a JAK2 mutation in every line.

steps.x: **C. Clonal disorder of a haematopoietic stem cell.** MPN = clonal stem cell disorder; one or more lines overproduced.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has primary myelofibrosis. His trephine biopsy shows clusters of abnormal megakaryocytes surrounded by dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis. The fibroblasts themselves are not part of the malignant clone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the marrow fibrosis?
o: Cytokines from clonal megakaryocytes stimulate fibroblasts
questions.e: Abnormal megakaryocyte and granulocyte clones release PDGF and TGF-beta, which stimulate (non-clonal) fibroblasts, causing progressive fibrosis and marrow failure.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: not part of the malignant clone
steps.x: The fibrosis is a reaction by normal fibroblasts to signals from the clone.

elim: The stem shows fibroblasts are not part of the clone.
Not the mechanism.
Amyloid is not reticulin or collagen fibrosis.
No history of radiation.

steps.x: **A. Cytokines from clonal megakaryocytes stimulate fibroblasts.** PMF fibrosis: PDGF and TGF-beta from clonal megakaryocytes.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with primary myelofibrosis has a spleen that reaches her right iliac fossa and a liver 6 cm below the costal margin. Her marrow is almost completely fibrosed. A splenic biopsy would show red cell, white cell and platelet precursors.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her massive splenomegaly?
questions.e: As the marrow fibroses, blood cell production shifts to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing massive hepatosplenomegaly.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: red cell, white cell and platelet precursors
steps.x: The marrow has failed; blood is being made elsewhere.

elim: She has myelofibrosis; precursors of all lines are present.
Would not put blood cell precursors in the spleen.
That is autoimmune haemolysis.
Gaucher disease.

steps.x: **A. Extramedullary haematopoiesis.** Massive spleen in PMF = extramedullary haematopoiesis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with primary myelofibrosis has a blood film showing many red cells shaped like teardrops. A student asks why the red cells have this shape.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Deformation of red cells leaving fibrotic marrow
Mechanical shearing on fibrin strands in vessels
Membrane cholesterol excess in liver disease
questions.e: Fibrotic marrow (and extramedullary sites) release immature and abnormally shaped red cells; squeezing out of a fibrotic marrow produces teardrop cells (dacrocytes).

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
Teardrop cells in myelofibrosis.

elim: Produces spherocytes.
Thalassaemia produces target cells.
Produces schistocytes.
Produces target cells and acanthocytes.

steps.x: **C. Deformation of red cells leaving fibrotic marrow.** Dacrocytes = red cells deformed by fibrotic marrow.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with essential thrombocythaemia has attacks of burning pain, warmth and redness in both feet, triggered by heat and exercise. His foot pulses are normal. Skin biopsy shows small arterioles blocked with platelet-rich thrombi.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his foot symptoms?
questions.e: In ET, clonal megakaryocytes make excessive, dysfunctional platelets that activate in small vessels, causing erythromelalgia.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
Microvascular platelet thrombi in ET.

elim: His foot pulses are normal.
The biopsy shows thrombi, not nerve damage.
He has ET, not PV.
Raynaud's causes cold, pale digits, not warm red feet.

steps.x: **B. Dysfunctional platelets occluding the microcirculation.** Erythromelalgia = dysfunctional platelets in the microcirculation (aspirin helps).
